label: Modern Indian History
blurb: From Plassey to Partition, ranked by exam frequency. Dates, sessions, pacts and the people who were actually in the room.

topics.title: Gandhi’s three mass movements and what triggered each
topics.hook: Non-Cooperation in 1920, Civil Disobedience in 1930, Quit India in 1942. Three movements, three triggers, three different ways of ending.
topics.story:
Gandhi returned from South Africa in **1915**. His first Indian campaigns were local: **Champaran (1917)** against indigo planters in Bihar, his first satyagraha in India; **Ahmedabad mill workers (1918)**, his first hunger strike; and **Kheda (1918)** against revenue collection after crop failure, his first non-cooperation.

**Non-Cooperation, 1920-22.** Triggered by the **Rowlatt Act (1919)**, which allowed detention without trial and was called the black act, and by the **Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 13 April 1919**, where General Dyer's troops fired on a crowd at Amritsar. The Khilafat grievance over the treatment of the Ottoman Caliph after the First World War brought Muslim leaders, the Ali brothers, into alliance. Adopted at the Nagpur session of 1920. Boycott of schools, courts, councils, foreign cloth and titles. Gandhi returned his Kaiser-i-Hind medal. It ended abruptly when a crowd burned a police station at **Chauri Chaura** in Gorakhpur on **5 February 1922**, killing 22 policemen; Gandhi suspended the movement on 12 February, to the anger of Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das and Subhas Bose.

**Civil Disobedience, 1930-34.** Triggered by the **Simon Commission (1927)**, an all-white statutory commission with no Indian member, met with "Simon Go Back"; by the rejection of the **Nehru Report (1928)**; and by the **Lahore session of December 1929**, which declared **Purna Swaraj** and fixed 26 January 1930 as Independence Day. Gandhi launched it with the **Dandi March**, 12 March to 6 April 1930, walking 240 miles from Sabarmati to break the salt law. Suspended by the **Gandhi-Irwin Pact of March 1931**, resumed after the second Round Table Conference failed, and called off in 1934.

**Quit India, 1942.** Triggered by the failure of the **Cripps Mission** and the advance of Japan. The resolution was passed in Bombay on **8 August 1942**; "Do or Die" was the slogan. The entire leadership was arrested within hours, and the movement was leaderless and largely spontaneous. Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank; Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia and Usha Mehta, who ran an underground radio, led from below.

facts.v: 12 March to 6 April 1930, 240 miles, Sabarmati to Dandi

topics.why: The reliable question is which event triggered which movement, and which movement was called off after which incident. Chauri Chaura and the Gandhi-Irwin Pact are the two the paper reaches for.

topics.title: The Revolt of 1857 and the end of Company rule
topics.hook: Started by sepoys over a rifle cartridge, spread into a rebellion of dispossessed rulers, and ended with the Crown taking India over directly.
topics.story:
The immediate cause was the **Enfield P-53 rifle**, whose cartridges were greased with animal fat and had to be bitten open. **Mangal Pandey** of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry attacked his officers at **Barrackpore on 29 March 1857** and was hanged on 8 April. The revolt proper began at **Meerut on 10 May 1857**, and the sepoys marched to Delhi and proclaimed the Mughal emperor **Bahadur Shah Zafar** as their leader.

Deeper causes: the **Doctrine of Lapse** under Dalhousie, which annexed Satara, Jhansi and Nagpur; the annexation of **Awadh in 1856** on grounds of misgovernment, which affected a large share of the Bengal Army's recruits; the **General Service Enlistment Act 1856** requiring sepoys to serve overseas; land settlements that dispossessed talukdars; and resentment at missionary activity and social legislation.

Centres and leaders: **Delhi**, Bahadur Shah Zafar with General Bakht Khan; **Kanpur**, Nana Sahib with Tantia Tope; **Lucknow**, Begum Hazrat Mahal; **Jhansi**, Rani Lakshmibai, who died fighting near Gwalior on 18 June 1858; **Bareilly**, Khan Bahadur Khan; **Bihar**, Kunwar Singh of Jagdishpur, then in his seventies; **Faizabad**, Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah.

The revolt failed. It was confined largely to the north, the Punjab and the south stayed quiet, the Sikh and Gurkha regiments sided with the British, and the leaders had no common programme. Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried and exiled to Rangoon, where he died in 1862, the last Mughal emperor.

The consequence was the **Government of India Act 1858**. The East India Company was abolished, the Board of Control and Court of Directors were replaced by a **Secretary of State for India** with a Council of fifteen, and the Governor-General became **Viceroy**, the first being **Lord Canning**. **Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1 November 1858**, read at Allahabad, promised non-interference in religion, the end of annexation, and equality of Indians in public office. The army was reorganised on a one-to-two European-to-Indian ratio, artillery kept in British hands, and recruitment shifted to declared "martial races".

facts.v: Greased cartridges of the Enfield P-53 rifle
Bahadur Shah Zafar, last Mughal emperor
Government of India Act 1858; Company rule ended

topics.why: Expect leader-and-centre matching, and the distinction between the immediate cause and the underlying ones. The Act of 1858 and the title Viceroy are the standard follow-up.

nodes.label: Lord Canning
nodes.note: Governor-General from 1856, first Viceroy from 1858. Called "Clemency Canning" for opposing indiscriminate reprisals.

nodes.label: Queen Victoria’s Proclamation
nodes.note: 1 November 1858. Non-interference in religion, no further annexation, equality in public employment. Called the Magna Carta of Indian liberties.

nodes.label: Rani Lakshmibai
nodes.note: Her state was annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse in 1854. Died in action near Gwalior, 18 June 1858.

nodes.label: Nana Sahib
nodes.note: Adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II, denied his pension. Tantia Tope was his general, captured and hanged in 1859.

nodes.label: Begum Hazrat Mahal
nodes.note: Led the revolt in Awadh in the name of her son Birjis Qadr, and later took refuge in Nepal.

nodes.label: Annexation of Awadh (1856)
nodes.note: Annexed on grounds of misgovernment. A large part of the Bengal Army was recruited from Awadh, which spread resentment through the ranks.

nodes.label: Kunwar Singh
nodes.note: Zamindar of Jagdishpur, in his seventies, who led the revolt in Bihar and died in April 1858.

nodes.label: Army reorganisation
nodes.note: Ratio of European to Indian troops raised, artillery reserved to Europeans, and recruitment concentrated on "martial races".

nodes.label: Martial race theory
nodes.note: Sikhs, Gurkhas, Rajputs and Punjabi Muslims favoured after 1857 because their regiments had stayed loyal.

nodes.label: V.D. Savarkar
nodes.note: His 1909 book called the revolt "The Indian War of Independence, 1857". British writers called it a sepoy mutiny.

topics.title: The Congress: founding, the sessions that matter, and the 1907 split
topics.hook: Founded by a retired British civil servant in 1885, split at Surat in 1907, reunited at Lucknow in 1916, and led by a different person almost every year.
topics.story:
The Indian National Congress was founded in **December 1885** at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, **Bombay**, by **A.O. Hume**, a retired Scottish member of the Indian Civil Service. Its first session had 72 delegates and was presided over by **W.C. Bonnerjee**. The Viceroy at the time was **Lord Dufferin**. The "safety valve" theory, that Hume founded it with British approval to channel discontent, comes from Lala Lajpat Rai and is contested.

**Moderates, 1885 to 1905.** Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Surendranath Banerjee, Pherozeshah Mehta, W.C. Bonnerjee. Their method was petition, prayer and protest; their achievement was the economic critique of empire. **Dadabhai Naoroji**, the Grand Old Man of India, developed the **drain of wealth** theory in *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India* (1901), and was the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons, in 1892, for Central Finsbury.

**Extremists, 1905 to 1920.** Lal-Bal-Pal: **Lala Lajpat Rai**, **Bal Gangadhar Tilak** and **Bipin Chandra Pal**, with Aurobindo Ghosh. Tilak's line, "Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it", is the most quoted sentence of the period. The trigger was the **Partition of Bengal**, announced by Curzon in July 1905 and effective 16 October 1905, which produced the **Swadeshi and Boycott** movement. The partition was annulled in 1911, when the capital also moved from Calcutta to Delhi.

**Sessions worth memorising.** 1885 Bombay, W.C. Bonnerjee, the first. 1886 Calcutta, Dadabhai Naoroji. 1887 Madras, Badruddin Tyabji, the first Muslim president. 1907 **Surat**, the split between Moderates and Extremists. 1916 **Lucknow**, reunion of the two factions and the **Lucknow Pact** with the Muslim League, accepting separate electorates. 1917 Calcutta, **Annie Besant**, the first woman president. 1920 Nagpur, Non-Cooperation adopted. 1924 Belgaum, the only session Gandhi presided over. 1925 Kanpur, **Sarojini Naidu**, the first Indian woman president. 1929 **Lahore**, Jawaharlal Nehru, Purna Swaraj. 1938 Haripura and 1939 Tripuri, **Subhas Chandra Bose**, who won at Tripuri against Gandhi's candidate Pattabhi Sitaramayya and then resigned, founding the **Forward Bloc** in 1939.

facts.v: Lucknow session, 1916, with the Lucknow Pact

topics.why: Session, year, place and president is a four-part matching question that appears constantly. Learn the ten listed here and you cover most of what is ever asked.

nodes.label: A.O. Hume
nodes.note: Retired Scottish ICS officer, ornithologist. General Secretary of the Congress for its first twenty-two years.

nodes.label: Surat split (1907)
nodes.note: Moderates and Extremists split over the presidency and the pace of agitation. They reunited only in 1916.

nodes.note: Reunited the factions and produced the Congress-League pact, in which the Congress accepted separate electorates.

nodes.note: Drain of wealth theory. First Indian in the British House of Commons, 1892. Congress president three times.

nodes.label: Bal Gangadhar Tilak

nodes.label: W.C. Bonnerjee
nodes.note: Presided over the first session of 72 delegates at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay.

nodes.label: Badruddin Tyabji
nodes.note: Presided at Madras in 1887. Later a judge of the Bombay High Court.

nodes.label: Sarojini Naidu
nodes.note: First Indian woman Congress president, Kanpur 1925. Later the first woman Governor of an Indian province, United Provinces.

nodes.label: Lahore session (1929)
nodes.note: Presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru. The tricolour was unfurled on the banks of the Ravi at midnight on 31 December 1929.

topics.title: From Cripps to Partition: the missions, plans and the Act of 1947
topics.hook: Four attempts to settle the constitutional question in five years, and the one that finally worked did it by dividing the country.
topics.story:
**August Offer, 1940.** Made by Viceroy Linlithgow. Dominion status after the war and an expanded Executive Council. Rejected by both the Congress and the League.

**Cripps Mission, March 1942.** Sir Stafford Cripps offered dominion status after the war and the right of provinces to opt out of the union. Gandhi's verdict, "a post-dated cheque", is the standard quotation. Its failure led directly to Quit India.

**Wavell Plan and Simla Conference, June 1945.** Proposed an Executive Council with equal Hindu and Muslim representation. Collapsed when **Jinnah** insisted the League alone could nominate Muslim members.

**Cabinet Mission, March 1946.** Three members: **Pethick-Lawrence** (Secretary of State), **Stafford Cripps** and **A.V. Alexander**. It rejected Pakistan and proposed a three-tier federation with provinces grouped into sections, a weak centre handling defence, foreign affairs and communications, and a Constituent Assembly. Both parties accepted it initially with different interpretations, then the League withdrew and called **Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946**, which set off the Great Calcutta Killings. The Constituent Assembly nevertheless met on 9 December 1946 under this plan.

**Mountbatten Plan, 3 June 1947.** Louis Mountbatten arrived in March 1947 as the last Viceroy, replacing Wavell, with a mandate to transfer power by June 1948; he advanced the date to August 1947. The plan provided for partition, referendums in the North West Frontier Province and Sylhet, and the right of princely states to accede to either dominion.

**Indian Independence Act 1947.** Received royal assent on **18 July 1947**. Created two independent dominions from **15 August 1947**, ended British paramountcy over the princely states, and made each dominion's Constituent Assembly its legislature. The **Radcliffe Line**, drawn by **Cyril Radcliffe** who had never visited India before, divided Punjab and Bengal; the awards were published on 17 August, two days after independence.

Integration of the princely states was managed by **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel** with **V.P. Menon**. Three held out: **Junagadh**, settled by plebiscite in February 1948; **Hyderabad**, taken by Operation Polo in September 1948; and **Jammu and Kashmir**, which acceded on 26 October 1947 after a Pakistani tribal invasion.

facts.v: Louis Mountbatten; first Governor-General of independent India

timeline.what: Cabinet Mission; Direct Action Day, 16 August
Junagadh plebiscite; Operation Polo in Hyderabad

topics.why: Mission-to-year matching is a standard question, and so is who was in the Cabinet Mission. The trap is confusing the Cripps Mission with the Cabinet Mission, both of which included Stafford Cripps.

topics.title: Company rule: Plassey, Buxar, and how land revenue was settled
topics.hook: A battle won by bribery in 1757, a battle won properly in 1764, and three revenue systems that shaped rural India for two centuries.
topics.story:
**Battle of Plassey, 23 June 1757.** **Robert Clive** defeated **Siraj-ud-Daulah**, Nawab of Bengal, after buying off his commander **Mir Jafar**, who was installed in his place. The fighting was slight; the consequence was that the Company became the effective power in Bengal.

**Battle of Buxar, 22 October 1764.** Hector Munro defeated the combined forces of **Mir Qasim**, **Shuja-ud-Daulah** of Awadh and the Mughal emperor **Shah Alam II**. This was the decisive military victory. The **Treaty of Allahabad (1765)** gave the Company the **Diwani**, the right to collect revenue in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, in exchange for an annual payment to the emperor. The result was the **dual government** in Bengal, revenue with the Company and administration with the Nawab, which Warren Hastings ended in 1772.

**Regulating Act 1773.** The first parliamentary intervention. Made the Governor of Bengal the **Governor-General of Bengal**, the first being **Warren Hastings**, with a council of four, and set up a Supreme Court at Calcutta in 1774. **Pitt's India Act 1784** created the **Board of Control**, establishing dual control by the Company and the Crown.

**Charter Acts.** 1813 ended the Company's monopoly of Indian trade except in tea and with China, and allowed missionaries in. 1833 ended commercial activity entirely, made the Governor-General of Bengal the **Governor-General of India**, the first being **William Bentinck**, and provided for a Law Commission, which produced Macaulay's penal code. 1853 introduced open competition for the civil service.

**Land revenue systems.** The **Permanent Settlement**, introduced by **Cornwallis in 1793** in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, fixed the revenue demand in perpetuity and made zamindars proprietors; covering about 19% of British India, it produced absentee landlordism. The **Ryotwari system**, associated with **Thomas Munro** in Madras and **Alexander Read**, settled revenue directly with the cultivator and covered about 51%. The **Mahalwari system**, introduced by **Holt Mackenzie** in 1822 in the North-Western Provinces and revised by **William Bentinck**, settled with the village or mahal collectively and covered about 30%.

facts.v: 1765; Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa
Warren Hastings, under the Regulating Act 1773
William Bentinck, under the Charter Act 1833

topics.why: Plassey against Buxar is the classic trap: Plassey made the Company powerful, Buxar made it legitimate. Revenue systems are matched to their author and region.

nodes.label: Permanent Settlement (1793)

nodes.label: Regulating Act, 1773
nodes.note: Created the Governor-General of Bengal and a Supreme Court at Calcutta. Warren Hastings was the first holder.

nodes.label: Pitt’s India Act, 1784
nodes.note: Created the Board of Control, giving the Crown authority over political matters while the Company kept commerce.

nodes.label: Charter Act, 1833
nodes.note: Made Bentinck Governor-General of India, ended the Company’s commercial functions, and provided for a Law Commission.

nodes.label: Robert Clive
nodes.note: Twice Governor of Bengal. Introduced the dual government in 1765. Impeached in Britain and died in 1774.

nodes.label: Warren Hastings

nodes.label: Macaulay’s Minute (1835)
nodes.note: Argued for English education. Bentinck’s resolution made English the medium of instruction and the language of the higher courts.

nodes.label: Dual government
nodes.note: Revenue with the Company, administration with the Nawab. Neither was accountable, and the Bengal famine of 1770 followed.

topics.title: Social and religious reform movements and their founders
topics.hook: A matching question waiting to happen: nine movements, nine founders, nine years, and the reforms each of them pushed through.
topics.story:
**Brahmo Samaj**, founded by **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** in **1828** in Calcutta, originally as the Brahmo Sabha. Monotheistic, against idolatry and caste. Roy campaigned successfully for the abolition of **sati**, which Bentinck banned by regulation in **1829**. Debendranath Tagore and later **Keshab Chandra Sen** led it; Sen's faction pushed the **Native Marriage Act 1872**, which set minimum marriage ages.

**Prarthana Samaj**, Bombay, **1867**, founded by Atmaram Pandurang and led by **M.G. Ranade** and R.G. Bhandarkar. Focused on widow remarriage and women's education rather than doctrine.

**Arya Samaj**, founded by **Swami Dayanand Saraswati** in **1875** in Bombay. Slogan: "Back to the Vedas". Rejected idol worship, child marriage and untouchability, and began **shuddhi**, reconversion. His book is *Satyarth Prakash*.

**Ramakrishna Mission**, founded by **Swami Vivekananda** in **1897** at Belur, in memory of his teacher **Ramakrishna Paramahansa**. Vivekananda's address to the **Parliament of Religions in Chicago on 11 September 1893** is the standard reference.

**Theosophical Society**, founded in New York in **1875** by **Madame H.P. Blavatsky** and **Colonel H.S. Olcott**, moved its headquarters to **Adyar, Madras, in 1882**. **Annie Besant** later led it and founded the Central Hindu College at Banaras in 1898, which grew into Banaras Hindu University under Madan Mohan Malaviya.

**Aligarh Movement**, **Sir Syed Ahmad Khan**, who founded the Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh in **1875**, later Aligarh Muslim University. Argued for modern education and against Muslim participation in the Congress.

**Satyashodhak Samaj**, founded by **Jyotiba Phule** in **1873** in Pune, against Brahminical dominance. With **Savitribai Phule** he opened the first school for girls in Pune in 1848. His book is *Gulamgiri* (1873).

**Self-Respect Movement**, **E.V. Ramasamy, Periyar**, Tamil Nadu, **1925**. **Sri Narayana Guru** led the Ezhava movement in Kerala with the slogan "One caste, one religion, one God for man"; the **Vaikom Satyagraha** of 1924-25 over temple-road access grew out of it.

Legislation to remember: **Sati abolished 1829**; **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act 1856**, pushed by **Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar**; **Age of Consent Act 1891**; **Sharda Act 1929**, raising the marriage age to 14 for girls and 18 for boys.

facts.v: Swami Dayanand Saraswati, 1875, "Back to the Vedas"
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, MAO College 1875
1929, marriage age 14 for girls and 18 for boys

topics.why: Founder-movement-year matching is asked almost every year, often paired with one social legislation date. Learn Roy with 1828 and sati with 1829, and the rest follows.

nodes.label: Swami Vivekananda
nodes.note: Founded 1897 at Belur. His Chicago address of 11 September 1893 opened with "Sisters and brothers of America".

nodes.label: Jyotiba Phule
nodes.note: Founded 1873. Opened the first school for girls in Pune in 1848 with Savitribai Phule. Wrote Gulamgiri.

nodes.label: Abolition of sati (1829)

nodes.label: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan
nodes.note: Founded the Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College in 1875, which became Aligarh Muslim University in 1920.

nodes.label: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar

nodes.label: Theosophical Society
nodes.note: Founded in New York by Blavatsky and Olcott, headquarters at Adyar from 1882. Annie Besant later president.

nodes.label: E.V. Ramasamy Periyar
nodes.note: Founded 1925 in Tamil Nadu. Anti-caste and rationalist; later founded the Dravidar Kazhagam.

nodes.label: Sri Narayana Guru
nodes.note: "One caste, one religion, one God for man." Founded the SNDP Yogam in Kerala in 1903.

nodes.label: Vaikom Satyagraha (1924-25)
nodes.note: Campaign for lower-caste access to roads around the Vaikom temple in Travancore. Gandhi visited in 1925.

nodes.label: Prarthana Samaj
nodes.note: Bombay, founded by Atmaram Pandurang, led by M.G. Ranade and R.G. Bhandarkar.

nodes.label: Sharda Act (1929)
nodes.note: Child Marriage Restraint Act. Marriage age set at 14 for girls and 18 for boys, raised later.

nodes.label: Annie Besant
nodes.note: Founded the Home Rule League in 1916 and the Central Hindu College at Banaras in 1898.

nodes.label: Keshab Chandra Sen
nodes.note: His faction secured the Native Marriage Act 1872, setting minimum ages for marriage.

passages.title: The movement called off
passages.passage:
The movement launched at the end of 1920 was the first attempt to make Indian nationalism a mass affair rather than a conversation between lawyers. Its programme was withdrawal: students left government schools, lawyers gave up practice, voters boycotted the new councils, and foreign cloth was burned in public. Two grievances had brought an unusual coalition together. One was a wartime security law that permitted detention without trial, and the massacre at Amritsar that followed the protests against it. The other was the treatment of the Ottoman Caliph after the war, which mobilised Muslim opinion behind a leadership that had until then kept its distance from the Congress.

For about eighteen months the movement grew. Then, in February 1922, a procession in a small town in the United Provinces was fired upon by police, turned on the police station, and burned it with twenty-two policemen inside. Within a week the leader of the movement had suspended it entirely, arguing that a people not yet capable of discipline under provocation could not be trusted with a mass campaign. He was arrested the following month, tried for sedition, and sentenced to six years.

The suspension split the leadership. Two senior figures who had given up lucrative legal practices to join the campaign formed a new party to contest the very council elections the movement had boycotted, on the argument that obstruction from inside the councils was better than nothing at all. A younger leader from Bengal never forgave the decision and would spend the next two decades arguing that the struggle needed methods the leadership was unwilling to countenance.

The alliance that had made the movement possible did not survive either. The grievance that had brought it about was resolved not in India but in Turkey, where the Caliphate was abolished in 1924 by a government with no interest in Indian opinion.

questions.q: The town where the police station was burned in February 1922 is:
questions.explain: Chauri Chaura in Gorakhpur district, on 5 February 1922. Champaran and Kheda were 1917-18 satyagrahas; Bardoli was the 1928 no-tax campaign led by Vallabhbhai Patel.

questions.q: The wartime security law referred to in the first paragraph is the:
questions.explain: The Rowlatt Act of 1919, popularly summarised as "no vakil, no appeal, no daleel". The protests against it led to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre on 13 April 1919.

questions.q: The new party formed by the two senior figures described in the third paragraph was the:
questions.explain: The Swaraj Party, founded in 1923 by Motilal Nehru and C.R. Das to contest council elections. The Forward Bloc was founded by Subhas Chandra Bose in 1939.

questions.q: The younger leader from Bengal referred to in the same paragraph is most likely:
questions.explain: Subhas Chandra Bose, who criticised the suspension and later broke with Gandhi over methods, eventually leading the Indian National Army.

questions.q: Which statement about the alliance described in the passage is accurate?
options: It ended when the Congress withdrew from it in 1922
It ended because the Caliphate was abolished in Turkey in 1924
It was never formally agreed to by Muslim leaders
It continued until the Lucknow Pact of 1916
questions.explain: The Khilafat cause collapsed when Mustafa Kemal’s government abolished the Caliphate in 1924. The Lucknow Pact of 1916 predates this movement entirely.
